turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Well, the main reason I’m here is that I'm having a lot of trouble at work. I'm a nurse, and when I'm on the floor, I just lose my train of thought constantly. 

It happens all the time—an IV pump will beep, or I'll overhear someone asking another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was just working on. It's really becoming a major problem for me.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes losing their train of thought constantly due to extraneous stimuli like IV pumps beeping, call lights, and other people's conversations.

turns.doctor_question: When you're not at work—say, at home relaxing or doing personal activities—do you notice the same difficulty concentrating and losing your train of thought, or does it mainly happen during your shifts?
turns.patient_response: I'm actually not sure. I haven't really noticed it happening like that at home. I mean, when I'm just relaxing or doing my own thing, there isn't really as much pressure or as many things going on, so... I just don't know if I lose my train of thought the same way. It's really just during my shifts that it stands out to me as this massive problem.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had these concentration problems for most of your life, or did they start relatively recently—maybe in the last few months or years?
turns.patient_response: It's been most of my life, honestly. Even back in elementary school, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was bright but... careless. I was always losing my worksheets or just completely forgetting to turn in my homework. My mom actually had to sit down with me every single night just to keep me on track and make sure I got things done. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient notes that teachers described them as 'careless' on report cards.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient required their mother to sit with them every night to 'keep me on track', indicating difficulty sustaining attention independently.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient needed their mother's help to 'make sure I got things done', implying a failure to finish schoolwork on their own.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they were 'always losing my worksheets'.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient reports 'completely forgetting to turn in my homework', demonstrating forgetfulness in daily school activities.

turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced any recent changes in your health, such as new medical conditions, head injuries, sleep problems, or changes in any medications you might be taking?
turns.patient_response: No, nothing like that. My health has been fine. I haven't had any head injuries or new medical problems, and I'm not taking any new medications. My sleep is pretty normal, too. So, no recent changes there.

symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient explicitly states that their sleep is pretty normal, denying any sleep disturbances.

turns.doctor_question: Besides the carelessness your teachers noted, did you have trouble sitting still, staying organized, or getting things done without reminders when you were a child?
turns.patient_response: I don't really remember having trouble sitting still. I wasn't, you know, bouncing off the walls or anything. But staying organized and getting things done... yeah, that was always a struggle. Like I said, my mom had to sit with me every night just to make sure I actually finished my homework. Without her reminding me and kind of hovering, I just wouldn't get it done. My desk at school was always a disaster, too. So, the organization and needing reminders were definitely big issues, but I wasn't hyper.

turns.doctor_question: Growing up, did people ever describe you as impulsive or someone who acted without thinking things through first? For example, did you interrupt people, blurt things out, or do things without considering the consequences?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I wasn't the type to blurt things out or interrupt people. I was actually pretty quiet in class, usually just zoning out or daydreaming. I didn't really do things without thinking, either. It was more just... forgetting to do things at all, rather than doing them impulsively.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies being the type to blurt things out.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting people.

turns.doctor_question: At work as a nurse, do you find yourself making careless mistakes—like miscalculating medication doses, mixing up patient information, or overlooking important details in charts—even when you're trying to be careful?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do. It's... it's actually becoming a real problem. I try so hard to be careful, but I still make these careless mistakes. Like, I'll think I've completely finished an EHR audit or double-checked a transfer note, and I feel good about it. But then my supervisor will pull me aside and point out that I missed a required field, or I put the wrong time down for a medication follow-up. 

The worst is when I copy down the wrong room number. I swear I look right at it, and I think I've got it right, but then it turns out I wrote something completely different. It's incredibly frustrating because I know how important these details are, but they just seem to slip past me no matter how hard I focus.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly confirms making careless mistakes at work, such as missing required fields, putting the wrong time for medication follow-ups, and copying down the wrong room numbers despite trying to be careful.

turns.patient_response: No, not really. When I'm doing something I actually want to do, like reading a book I like or watching a show, I don't really have a problem focusing.
